subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Find the patterns behind everyday numbers.

lessons.title: Equivalent ratios
lessons.text: A ratio compares quantities. If a smoothie uses 2 cups of berries for 3 cups of yogurt, doubling both quantities gives 4:6. Multiplying both parts by the same number keeps the ratio equivalent.
lessons.q: A recipe uses 2 cups of rice for 3 cups of water. How much water goes with 6 cups of rice?
lessons.hint: 6 is three times 2. Multiply the water amount by that same factor.

lessons.title: Unit rates
lessons.text: A unit rate tells you how much for one. Divide the total amount by the number of units. For example, 20 kilometers in 4 hours is 5 kilometers per hour.
lessons.q: Five notebooks cost $15. What is the price per notebook?
lessons.hint: Divide the total price by the number of notebooks.

lessons.title: Apply proportional thinking
lessons.text: In a proportional relationship, the unit rate stays constant. Once you know the amount for one unit, multiply to find the amount for any number of units.
lessons.q: A bike travels 12 kilometers in 1 hour at a constant speed. How far does it travel in 2.5 hours?
lessons.hint: Find the distance in 2 hours, then add the distance in half an hour.

subjects.name: Language arts
subjects.description: Build stronger arguments, one idea at a time.

lessons.title: Make an inference
lessons.text: An inference combines clues in a text with what you already know. Read: “Maya folded her umbrella and left her muddy boots by the door.” The author never states the weather directly, but gives you clues.
options: Maya has been outside in wet weather.
lessons.hint: Look at what an umbrella and muddy boots suggest together.
lessons.why: The umbrella and muddy boots both support the inference of wet weather.

lessons.title: Find the evidence
lessons.text: A claim becomes stronger when specific evidence supports it. “The garden attracts wildlife” is a claim. A count of visiting animals can support it more directly than an opinion about the garden.
lessons.q: Which observation best supports the claim that a garden attracts wildlife?
options: Six species of birds visited this week.
lessons.hint: Choose the observation that directly describes wildlife.
lessons.why: The bird count is direct, specific evidence of wildlife visiting.

lessons.title: Recognize a counterargument
lessons.text: A counterargument offers a reason to question a claim. Understanding one helps you improve your own reasoning. A proposal for longer recess might be challenged by a concern about less classroom time.
lessons.q: Which is a counterargument to “All homework should be online”?
options: Some students lack reliable internet at home.
lessons.hint: Which choice gives a reason to question the proposal?
lessons.why: Unequal internet access challenges whether online-only homework works for every student.

subjects.name: Science
subjects.description: Turn your curiosity into a testable idea.

lessons.title: Ask a testable question
lessons.text: A testable question can be investigated using observations or measurements. “Does light affect plant growth?” can be tested by changing light exposure and measuring growth.
lessons.q: Which question can be tested with measurements?
options: Do bean plants grow taller with 8 hours of light than with 4?
lessons.hint: Choose a question with a change you can make and a result you can measure.
lessons.why: You can control hours of light and measure plant height.

lessons.title: Control the variables
lessons.text: For a fair comparison, change one factor and keep other relevant conditions the same. When testing light exposure, use the same plant type, soil, and watering schedule.
lessons.q: When testing light exposure, which factor should you deliberately change?
lessons.hint: The factor you change should match the question you are testing.
lessons.why: Changing only light makes it easier to connect differences in growth to light exposure.

lessons.title: Interpret the results
lessons.text: Evidence supports conclusions within the limits of an experiment. Repeated trials help you see whether a pattern is consistent; one observation rarely settles a question.
lessons.q: One plant grows taller under a brighter lamp. What should you do next?
options: Claim all plants need the brightest lamp.
Repeat with more plants under controlled conditions.
lessons.hint: Think about how to check whether the pattern is reliable.
lessons.why: Repeating a controlled experiment helps test whether the result is consistent.

projects.title: Turn a small idea into a big possibility.
projects.description: Spot a problem in your world. Design something that makes it better.
steps: Name a small problem in your school or community.
Describe who experiences it and interview someone, with a trusted adult’s help.
Sketch a solution and estimate the materials it needs.
Give a 60-second pitch: problem, solution, and who it helps.

projects.title: Make your voice heard.
projects.description: Tell a true story that helps someone see your point of view.
steps: Choose a moment when you learned something.
Write a beginning, a challenge, and what changed.
Practice telling the story in two minutes.
Ask a trusted listener what they remembered.
